claim: The temperature of active mitochondria in four mammalian and one insect cell line was estimated to be up to 15°C above that of the external environment to which the cells were exposed, based on studies with Mito Thermo Yellow (MTY) and the genetically encoded gTEMP ratiometric fluorescent temperature indicator.
source: Based on studies with a fluorescent reporter dye, Mito Thermo Yellow (MTY), and the genetically encoded gTEMP ratiometric fluorescent temperature indicator targeted to mitochondria, the temperature of active mitochondria in four mammalian and one insect cell line was estimated to be up to 15°C above that of the external environment to which the cells were exposed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using two different fluorescent temperature measurement methods (MTY and gTEMP) across multiple cell lines, as described throughout the manuscript.

claim: High mitochondrial temperature was maintained in the face of substrate starvation or modification.
source: High mitochondrial temperature was maintained in the face of a variety of metabolic stresses, including substrate starvation or modification, decreased ATP demand due to inhibition of cytosolic protein synthesis, inhibition of the mitochondrial adenine nucleotide transporter and, if an auxiliary pathway for electron transfer was available via the alternative oxidase, even respiratory poisons acting downstream of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complex I.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing mitochondrial temperature maintenance under various metabolic stress conditions, as detailed in Figure 5 and related text.

claim: High mitochondrial temperature was maintained when ATP demand was decreased due to inhibition of cytosolic protein synthesis.
source: High mitochondrial temperature was maintained in the face of a variety of metabolic stresses, including substrate starvation or modification, decreased ATP demand due to inhibition of cytosolic protein synthesis, inhibition of the mitochondrial adenine nucleotide transporter and, if an auxiliary pathway for electron transfer was available via the alternative oxidase, even respiratory poisons acting downstream of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complex I.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using anisomycin to inhibit cytosolic protein synthesis, as shown in Figure 7.

claim: High mitochondrial temperature was maintained following inhibition of the mitochondrial adenine nucleotide transporter.
source: High mitochondrial temperature was maintained in the face of a variety of metabolic stresses, including substrate starvation or modification, decreased ATP demand due to inhibition of cytosolic protein synthesis, inhibition of the mitochondrial adenine nucleotide transporter and, if an auxiliary pathway for electron transfer was available via the alternative oxidase, even respiratory poisons acting downstream of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complex I.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using bongkrekic acid (BKA) to inhibit the adenine nucleotide transporter, as shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: When an auxiliary pathway for electron transfer was available via the alternative oxidase, high mitochondrial temperature was maintained even in the presence of respiratory poisons acting downstream of OXPHOS complex I.
source: High mitochondrial temperature was maintained in the face of a variety of metabolic stresses, including substrate starvation or modification, decreased ATP demand due to inhibition of cytosolic protein synthesis, inhibition of the mitochondrial adenine nucleotide transporter and, if an auxiliary pathway for electron transfer was available via the alternative oxidase, even respiratory poisons acting downstream of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complex I.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AOX-expressing cells treated with various OXPHOS inhibitors, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: The high temperature of active mitochondria is an inescapable consequence of the biochemistry of OXPHOS.
source: We propose that the high temperature of active mitochondria is an inescapable consequence of the biochemistry of OXPHOS and is homeostatically maintained as a primary feature of mitochondrial metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings, proposing a mechanistic explanation for the observed high mitochondrial temperature.

claim: High mitochondrial temperature is homeostatically maintained as a primary feature of mitochondrial metabolism.
source: We propose that the high temperature of active mitochondria is an inescapable consequence of the biochemistry of OXPHOS and is homeostatically maintained as a primary feature of mitochondrial metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental observations of temperature maintenance under various metabolic stresses.

claim: The mitochondrial system of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is considered the most efficient energy conversion platform of non-photosynthetic eukaryotes.
source: The mitochondrial system of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is considered the most efficient energy conversion platform of non-photosynthetic eukaryotes.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about OXPHOS efficiency in eukaryotic cells.

claim: OXPHOS does not operate at or anywhere near 100% thermodynamic efficiency.
source: However, it does not operate at or anywhere near 100% thermodynamic efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by references to established scientific literature on OXPHOS thermodynamic efficiency.

claim: Much of the free energy released by the reoxidation of primary electron carriers such as NADH is converted to heat under normal physiological conditions.
source: Much of the free energy released by the reoxidation of primary electron carriers such as NADH is converted to heat. Note that this applies under normal physiological conditions (Kang, 2018; Brand, 2005; Nath, 2016), not only in cells expressing uncoupler proteins or treated with a chemical uncoupler.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous scientific literature on mitochondrial heat production.

claim: Mitochondrial heat production is not mere 'waste', since it is a major and regulatable energy source for maintaining body temperature in homeotherms such as mammals and birds.
source: Furthermore, this heat production is not mere 'waste', since it is a major and regulatable energy source for maintaining body temperature in homeotherms such as mammals and birds (Brand et al., 1994), and possibly many other organisms, even those living at a wide range of temperatures in varying environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brand et al., 1994, and represents established knowledge about thermoregulation.

claim: Uncoupler proteins serve an auxiliary function under cold stress in mice.
source: Uncoupler proteins merely serve an auxiliary function under cold stress, as shown by the fact that, in mice, ablation of the major uncoupling protein UCP1 is nonlethal (Enerbäck et al., 1997) and does not affect basal body temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enerbäck et al., 1997, showing that UCP1 knockout mice are viable.

claim: In mice, ablation of the major uncoupling protein UCP1 is nonlethal and does not affect basal body temperature.
source: Uncoupler proteins merely serve an auxiliary function under cold stress, as shown by the fact that, in mice, ablation of the major uncoupling protein UCP1 is nonlethal (Enerbäck et al., 1997) and does not affect basal body temperature.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by citation to Enerbäck et al., 1997.

claim: Using MTY, intramitochondrial temperature in respiring human HEK293-derived cells is at least 10–12°C higher than the ambient temperature at which the cells are maintained.
source: Using the mitochondrially targeted fluorescent dye Mito Thermo Yellow (MTY), it was recently shown that intramitochondrial temperature in respiring, human HEK293-derived (immortalised embryonic kidney) cells is at least 10–12°C higher than the ambient temperature at which the cells are maintained (Chrétien et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chrétien et al., 2018, a previous study by the authors.

claim: MTY fluorescence change after cells were treated with OXPHOS inhibitors indicated a temperature drop of 10-12°C magnitude, based on internal calibration.
source: In essence, this inference was based on the fact that the MTY fluorescence change, after cells were treated with OXPHOS inhibitors such as rotenone (targeted on OXPHOS complex I, cI), antimycin (targeted on OXPHOS complex III, cIII), or oligomycin (targeted on ATP synthase – OXPHOS complex V, cV), or subjected to prolonged anaerobiosis, indicated a temperature drop of this magnitude, based on internal calibration at the end of each experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chrétien et al., 2018, describing the methodology and findings of the previous study.

claim: Inferences from the use of protein-based fluorescence probes targeted to mitochondria are similar to those from MTY.
source: Inferences from the use of protein-based fluorescence probes targeted to mitochondria are similar (Nakano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nakano et al., 2017, which used protein-based temperature probes.

claim: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is at a temperature distinct from the extracellular environment.
source: In addition, similar methods have indicated that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Kriszt et al., 2017), cell nucleus (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), plasma membrane (Liang et al., 2022), and different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons (Tanimoto et al., 2016), are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kriszt et al., 2017.

claim: The cell nucleus is at a temperature distinct from the extracellular environment.
source: In addition, similar methods have indicated that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Kriszt et al., 2017), cell nucleus (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), plasma membrane (Liang et al., 2022), and different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons (Tanimoto et al., 2016), are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Okabe et al., 2012 and Hayashi et al., 2015.

claim: The plasma membrane is at a temperature distinct from the extracellular environment.
source: In addition, similar methods have indicated that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Kriszt et al., 2017), cell nucleus (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), plasma membrane (Liang et al., 2022), and different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons (Tanimoto et al., 2016), are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2022.

claim: Different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons, are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
source: In addition, similar methods have indicated that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Kriszt et al., 2017), cell nucleus (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), plasma membrane (Liang et al., 2022), and different cellular compartments, such as the cell body and neurites of neurons (Tanimoto et al., 2016), are at temperatures distinct from the extracellular environment and from each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tanimoto et al., 2016.

claim: The cells of many organisms, notably homeotherms, are unable to tolerate prolonged high or low temperatures when applied externally.
source: In particular, since the cells of many organisms, notably homeotherms, are unable to tolerate prolonged high or low temperatures when applied externally, the question arises as to how much the temperature of mitochondria is permitted to vary in vivo, and whether and how it is regulated according to physiological conditions (Lane, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular temperature tolerance, with a citation to Lane, 2018 for context.

claim: Mitochondrial temperature is physiologically maintained at ~15°C above ambient temperature.
source: Broadly, the outcome of these studies verifies that mitochondrial temperature is physiologically maintained at ~15°C above ambient temperature, and is subject to homeostatic regulation in response to metabolic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript using MTY and gTEMP methods.

claim: Mitochondrial temperature is subject to homeostatic regulation in response to metabolic stress.
source: Broadly, the outcome of these studies verifies that mitochondrial temperature is physiologically maintained at ~15°C above ambient temperature, and is subject to homeostatic regulation in response to metabolic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing temperature maintenance under various metabolic stresses, as shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: The fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature.
source: These trials showed that the fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), or pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), across the physiological range of these parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: MTY fluorescence is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration across the physiological range.
source: These trials showed that the fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), or pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), across the physiological range of these parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: MTY fluorescence is not responsive to changes in hydrogen peroxide across the physiological range.
source: These trials showed that the fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), or pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), across the physiological range of these parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: MTY fluorescence is not responsive to changes in pH across the physiological range.
source: These trials showed that the fluorescence signal of MTY in cell-free solution decreases almost linearly with temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), is not responsive to changes in calcium concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), or pH (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), across the physiological range of these parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: In most cell lines tested there was a clear gradation of mitochondrial temperature decrease using inhibitors that act progressively further along the OXPHOS chain: the effect was always greatest after oligomycin and generally least for rotenone, with potassium cyanide and antimycin intermediate.
source: In most cell lines tested there was a clear gradation of mitochondrial temperature decrease using inhibitors that act progressively further along the OXPHOS chain: the effect was always greatest after oligomycin (inhibitor of cV) and generally least for rotenone (cI inhibitor), with potassium cyanide (inhibitor of OXPHOS complex IV, cIV) and antimycin (cIII inhibitor) intermediate (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 across multiple cell lines.

claim: Oligomycin produced an implied temperature decrease of the order of 17–19°C in most cell lines.
source: In general, findings were similar for different cell lines, with an implied temperature decrease of the order of 17–19°C produced by oligomycin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from MTY fluorescence measurements across multiple cell lines, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Oligomycin-induced temperature decrease implies a mitochondrial temperature of at least 54°C, assuming that cV inhibition abolishes all mitochondrial heat production.
source: This implies a mitochondrial temperature of at least 54°C, assuming that cV inhibition abolishes all mitochondrial heat production, ±2°C, taking account of the possible slight deviation from linearity seen in the MTY fluorescence temperature-response curve at higher temperatures (dotted line, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and the assumption about oligomycin's effect, with reference to the calibration curve.

claim: Two different isolates of immortalised mouse embryonic fibroblasts (iMEFs) gave similar results in mitochondrial temperature measurements.
source: Two different isolates of immortalised mouse embryonic fibroblasts (iMEFs) gave similar results (Figure 2C and D), with no significant difference in the extent of mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone to inhibit cI or by antimycin to inhibit cIII (Figure 2C and D) or by a combination of the two drugs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing two iMEF lines, as shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: There was no significant difference in the extent of mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone or antimycin in two iMEF isolates.
source: Two different isolates of immortalised mouse embryonic fibroblasts (iMEFs) gave similar results (Figure 2C and D), with no significant difference in the extent of mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone to inhibit cI or by antimycin to inhibit cIII (Figure 2C and D) or by a combination of the two drugs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The inferred temperature of mitochondria in S2 cells from Drosophila, when suspended and oxygenated at 25°C, showed similar responses to OXPHOS inhibition as mammalian cells suspended at 37°C, except for oligomycin treatment.
source: The inferred temperature of mitochondria in S2 cells from the fruit-fly Drosophila, a poikilotherm, when suspended and oxygenated at 25°C, showed similar responses to OXPHOS inhibition as mammalian cells suspended at 37°C, except that we were unable to derive a stable reading after oligomycin treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D, panel i).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from S2 cells, as shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5D.

claim: MTY fluorescence was still increasing 2 hr after the addition of oligomycin to S2 cells, whereas other inhibitors gave a stable reading over the same time period.
source: MTY fluorescence was still increasing 2 hr after the addition of oligomycin, whereas other inhibitors, such as KCN, when applied to S2 cells, gave a stable reading over the same time period (e.g. Figure 2—figure supplement 5D, panel ii).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5D.

claim: Fluorescence reached a stable value after the addition of oligomycin in all cell lines tested except S2 cells.
source: Fluorescence reached a stable value after the addition of oligomycin in all of the other cell lines tested, e.g., U2OS human osteosarcoma cells as shown (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D, panel iii).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations across multiple cell lines, with U2OS shown as an example in Figure 2—figure supplement 5D, panel iii.

claim: Overnight growth in media predicted to stimulate mitochondrial as opposed to cytosolic ATP production had no effect on mitochondrial temperature.
source: We investigated the effect of culturing iMEF cells in low-glucose medium, with or without galactose supplementation, aiming to enhance dependence on mitochondrial respiration (Marroquin et al., 2007). This culture-medium alteration produced no significant change to the effect of cI inhibition on mitochondrial temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, with citation to Marroquin et al., 2007 for the rationale.

claim: The fluorescence of Sirius is highly temperature sensitive, declining as temperature rises, whereas that of mT-Sapphire is not.
source: The basis of the method is the fact that the fluorescence of Sirius is highly temperature sensitive, declining (like MTY) as temperature rises, whereas that of mT-Sapphire is not.
evidence: This describes the fundamental principle of the mito-gTEMP temperature measurement method, based on established knowledge from Nakano et al., 2017.

claim: The peak fluorescence ratio of mito-gTEMP is independent of expression level.
source: Since the two proteins are expressed at a fixed stoichiometry, the peak fluorescence ratio is independent of expression level, which may vary even within a cloned mammalian cell population (Pilbrough et al., 2009), as seen, for example, in Figure 3B.
evidence: This claim is based on the design of the mito-gTEMP construct and is supported by citation to Pilbrough et al., 2009 regarding expression variability, with visual evidence in Figure 3B.

claim: Oligomycin treatment of mito-gTEMP-expressing cell clones derived from three different mammalian cell lines gave extrapolated values for the mitochondrial temperature decrease in the same range as those inferred by MTY, although slightly (1–2°C) less in each case.
source: Oligomycin treatment of mito-gTEMP-expressing cell clones derived from three different mammalian cell lines gave extrapolated values for the mitochondrial temperature decrease in the same range as those inferred by MTY, although slightly (1–2°C) less in each case, implying an internal mitochondrial matrix temperature of ~52–54°C (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing MTY and mito-gTEMP methods across three cell lines, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The internal mitochondrial matrix temperature is ~52–54°C based on mito-gTEMP measurements.
source: Oligomycin treatment of mito-gTEMP-expressing cell clones derived from three different mammalian cell lines gave extrapolated values for the mitochondrial temperature decrease in the same range as those inferred by MTY, although slightly (1–2°C) less in each case, implying an internal mitochondrial matrix temperature of ~52–54°C (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from mito-gTEMP measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Rotenone treatment of iMEF(P) cells produced a similar amount of mitochondrial temperature decrease when estimated by mito-gTEMP as by MTY.
source: Rotenone treatment of iMEF(P) cells also produced a similar amount of mitochondrial temperature decrease when estimated by mito-gTEMP as by MTY (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the two methods in rotenone-treated cells, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The matrix localisation of GFP-related fluorescent reporters using the COX8 targeting peptide is well documented.
source: The matrix localisation of GFP-related fluorescent reporters using the COX8 targeting peptide is well documented (Molina and Shirihai, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Molina and Shirihai, 2009.

claim: At least some MTY interacts with the matrix protein aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2).
source: However, the exact intramitochondrial location of MTY is not known, besides the fact that at least some of it interacts with the matrix protein aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) (Arai et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arai et al., 2015.

claim: In mitochondrial subfractionation experiments, the mean proportion of MTY fluorescence retained in mitoplasts was 92%.
source: In the first fractionation step, mitoplasts were separated from the outer membrane space/IMS fraction. In two trials, the mean proportion of MTY fluorescence retained in mitoplasts was 92%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mitochondrial subfractionation experiments.

claim: In mitochondrial subfractionation experiments, the mean proportion of MTY fluorescence retained in the SMP fraction was 90%.
source: In the second fractionation step, mitoplasts were sonicated to prepare fractions enriched for matrix versus 'inside-out' sub-mitochondrial particles (SMPs). In two trials, the mean proportion of MTY fluorescence retained in the SMP fraction was 90%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mitochondrial subfractionation experiments.

claim: MTY is retained within, or closely associated with, the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: These findings are consistent with MTY being retained within, or closely associated with, the inner mitochondrial membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the subfractionation data showing MTY retention in SMPs.

claim: Mitochondria in individual cells were cooled to variable extents by oligomycin treatment.
source: Time-lapse imaging revealed that mitochondria in individual cells were cooled to variable extents by oligomycin treatment (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When mito-gTEMP-expressing iMEF cells were incubated in PBS at 37°C without any inhibitor, there was a modest but progressive decline in the fluorescence ratio over 35 min, indicating mitochondrial temperature was around 4°C lower than the peak value reached at approximately 10 min.
source: When mito-gTEMP-expressing iMEF cells were incubated in PBS at 37°C without the addition of any inhibitor, we observed that, after reaching a steady fluorescence ratio indicative of a temperature of 53–54°C, there was a modest but progressive decline in the fluorescence ratio, such that by 35 min of incubation the inferred mitochondrial temperature was around 4°C lower than the peak value reached at approximately 10 min (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In the complete absence of an externally supplied, metabolisable substrate, mitochondrial metabolism adjusts to a slightly lower heat output and steady-state temperature.
source: Although remaining much warmer than the surrounding medium, this suggests that, in the complete absence of an externally supplied, metabolisable substrate, mitochondrial metabolism adjusts to a slightly lower heat output and steady-state temperature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of temperature decline in PBS without substrates.

claim: The addition of glucose and glutamine enabled mitochondria to maintain a higher temperature of ~53°C at the end of the experiment.
source: As expected, this enabled mitochondria to maintain a higher temperature of ~53°C at the end of the experiment, although this was still slightly less than the initial temperature peak of ~55°C between 5 and 10 min of incubation (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The addition of glucose and glutamine at 10 min produced a small rise in mitochondrial temperature.
source: However, the addition of glucose and glutamine at 10 min did produce a small rise in mitochondrial temperature (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: Mitochondrial temperature fluctuates within a narrow range according to substrate supply.
source: In sum, these data indicate that mitochondrial temperature fluctuates within a narrow range according to substrate supply.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing temperature changes with substrate addition and removal.

claim: Cultured mouse fibroblasts respond to BKA by inducing glycolysis and downregulating mitochondrial respiration, whilst maintaining a high mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Previous investigators have shown that cultured mouse fibroblasts respond to BKA by inducing glycolysis and downregulating mitochondrial respiration, whilst maintaining a high mitochondrial membrane potential (Kano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kano et al., 2019.

claim: The mitochondrial temperature decrease observed after BKA treatment was minimal, following an apparent slight increase upon addition of the drug.
source: However, the mitochondrial temperature decrease that we observed was minimal, following an apparent slight increase upon addition of the drug (Figure 5E and F), qualitatively consistent with the MTY signal after discounting the quenching effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cells that principally metabolise cI-linked substrates, AOX makes only a minor contribution to respiratory electron flow under non-inhibited conditions.
source: In cells that principally metabolise cI-linked substrates, AOX makes only a minor contribution to respiratory electron flow under non-inhibited conditions (Szibor et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szibor et al., 2020.

claim: If cI is blocked, forcing cells to switch to other ubiquinone-linked substrates, AOX becomes engaged.
source: However, if cI is blocked, forcing cells to switch to other ubiquinone-linked substrates, AOX becomes engaged (Szibor et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szibor et al., 2020.

claim: The initial mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone in AOX-expressing iMEFs was very similar to that of control iMEFs.
source: Consistent with these expectations, the initial mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by the cI inhibitor rotenone in AOX-expressing iMEFs was very similar to that of control iMEFs, with a mitochondrial temperature decrease of ~10°C based on both MTY fluorescence (Figure 6A, panel i, Figure 6B) and the mito-gTEMP fluorescence ratio measured in iMEF cells stably transfected with AOX (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: After the initial temperature decrease from rotenone, AOX-expressing iMEFs showed gradual mitochondrial rewarming.
source: However, this was followed by a gradual mitochondrial rewarming (Figure 6A, panel i, Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, panel ii).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AOX-expressing iMEFs treated with other OXPHOS inhibitors showed a similar rewarming behaviour, except that the initial mitochondrial temperature decrease was substantially less than that seen in control iMEFs.
source: AOX-expressing iMEFs treated with other OXPHOS inhibitors showed a similar behaviour (Figure 6A panels ii–iv, Figure 6C), except that the initial mitochondrial temperature decrease was substantially less than that seen in control iMEFs (Figure 6A panels ii–iv, Figure 6B), whilst the rate and extent of rewarming differed according to the inhibitor used (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The rate and extent of mitochondrial rewarming in AOX-expressing iMEFs differed according to the inhibitor used.
source: AOX-expressing iMEFs treated with other OXPHOS inhibitors showed a similar behaviour (Figure 6A panels ii–iv, Figure 6C), except that the initial mitochondrial temperature decrease was substantially less than that seen in control iMEFs (Figure 6A panels ii–iv, Figure 6B), whilst the rate and extent of rewarming differed according to the inhibitor used (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Anisomycin treatment led to a transient slight increase in mitochondrial temperature (~4°C).
source: In contrast to our expectation that anisomycin, by attenuating ATP demand, would decrease electron flux in the OXPHOS system and thus lead to a drop in mitochondrial temperature, the latter instead showed a transient slight increase (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: High mitochondrial temperature was sustained for many hours after anisomycin treatment.
source: Thereafter, high mitochondrial temperature was sustained for many hours, although by 18 hr of exposure to the drug many of the cells were no longer attached and probably dying (the cells analysed in Figure 7A were those that had remained attached).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: AOX-expressing iMEF cells remained healthy-looking even after 18 hr in anisomycin.
source: AOX-expressing iMEF cells (Figure 7B) showed an almost identical behaviour, except that the cells remained healthy-looking even after 18 hr in anisomycin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The inferred mitochondrial temperature of anisomycin-treated iMEFs showed a lesser effect of rotenone than iMEFs not treated with anisomycin, and this effect was increasingly pronounced after longer times of anisomycin exposure.
source: The inferred mitochondrial temperature of anisomycin-treated iMEFs showed a lesser effect of rotenone than iMEFs not treated with anisomycin (Figure 7C, blue trace, compare 1–18 hr time-points with 0 hr control), and this effect was increasingly pronounced after longer times of anisomycin exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Mitochondrial temperature in surviving cells after 18 hr in anisomycin was almost unaffected by rotenone.
source: Mitochondrial temperature in the surviving cells after 18 hr in anisomycin was almost unaffected by rotenone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Anisomycin-exposed iMEFs were as affected by oligomycin as prior to treatment, even up to 18 hr.
source: In contrast, and despite some experiment-to-experiment variation, anisomycin-exposed iMEFs were as affected by oligomycin as prior to treatment, even up to 18 hr (Figure 7D, blue trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: After anisomycin treatment, AOX-expressing iMEFs showed a consistently greater mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone than did control iMEFs not expressing AOX.
source: AOX-expressing iMEFs behaved differently. After anisomycin treatment, they showed a consistently greater mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by rotenone (Figure 7C, red trace) than did control iMEFs not expressing AOX (Figure 7C, blue trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The mitochondria of anisomycin-treated iMEF(AOX) cells showed a temperature decrease by oligomycin significantly less than anisomycin-treated control iMEF(P) cells, regardless of the length of time of anisomycin exposure.
source: The mitochondria of anisomycin-treated iMEF(AOX) cells showed a temperature decrease by oligomycin significantly less than anisomycin-treated control iMEF(P) cells, regardless of the length of time of anisomycin exposure, but also showed a possibly increased effect of oligomycin, with increasing anisomycin exposure time (Figure 7D, red trace), at least for the first hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Anisomycin-exposed iMEF(AOX) cells showed the same slow rewarming after rotenone treatment as did iMEF(AOX) cells not exposed to anisomycin.
source: Anisomycin-exposed iMEF(AOX) cells showed the same slow rewarming after rotenone treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, panel i) as did iMEF(AOX) cells not exposed to anisomycin (Figure 6A panel i, Figure 6C), whilst control iMEFs did not show any such effect from rotenone (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, panel ii).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6.

claim: The rewarming effect after oligomycin treatment was slower and of much lower magnitude for anisomycin-treated than untreated iMEF(AOX) cells.
source: Conversely, the rewarming effect after oligomycin treatment was slower and of much lower magnitude for anisomycin-treated than untreated iMEF(AOX) cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), whilst a modest rewarming was also seen for control iMEFs not expressing AOX (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Much of the heat generated by OXPHOS is retained within the organelle, keeping mitochondrial temperature far above that of other cell components.
source: Our findings are inconsistent with this model, indicating instead that much of the heat generated by OXPHOS is retained within the organelle, keeping mitochondrial temperature far above that of other cell components and, whenever possible, within a narrow range.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings of high mitochondrial temperature.

claim: Heat conductance from the mitochondria might be modulated to maintain mitochondrial temperature.
source: Heat conductance from the mitochondria might also be modulated to maintain mitochondrial temperature.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism for temperature regulation.

claim: The use of a Peltier jacket surrounding the cuvette ensures that temperature changes in the cuvette rapidly and accurately reflect those applied.
source: The use of a Peltier jacket surrounding the cuvette in the apparatus ensures that temperature changes in the cuvette rapidly and accurately reflect those applied, as verified (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by validation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The MTY-based measurements may be slightly in error (by ~2°C), due to the minor deviation from linearity of the MTY fluorescence temperature-response curve, in the inferred temperature range of 50–60°C.
source: As stated earlier, the MTY-based measurements may be slightly in error (by ~2°C), due to the minor deviation from linearity of the MTY fluorescence temperature-response curve, in the inferred temperature range of 50–60°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the calibration data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Drugs that have different effects on mitochondrial membrane potential nevertheless all lead to a sustained increase in MTY fluorescence.
source: In previous studies it was argued that drugs that have different effects on mitochondrial membrane potential nevertheless all lead to a sustained increase in MTY fluorescence.
evidence: This refers to arguments made in previous studies, likely Chrétien et al., 2018.

claim: Treatment of cells with respiratory inhibitors such as rotenone or antimycin lead to substantially decreased membrane potential.
source: Treatment of cells with respiratory inhibitors such as rotenone or antimycin lead to substantially decreased membrane potential (Cannino et al., 2012; Kalbácová et al., 2003), whereas the effects of oligomycin on mitochondrial membrane potential are generally minor, and vary between cell lines and over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cannino et al., 2012 and Kalbácová et al., 2003.

claim: The effects of oligomycin on mitochondrial membrane potential are generally minor, and vary between cell lines and over time.
source: Treatment of cells with respiratory inhibitors such as rotenone or antimycin lead to substantially decreased membrane potential (Cannino et al., 2012; Kalbácová et al., 2003), whereas the effects of oligomycin on mitochondrial membrane potential are generally minor, and vary between cell lines and over time.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Kalbácová et al., 2003 and Yang et al., 2021.

claim: Oligomycin commonly results in a small increase in mitochondrial membrane potential, sometimes followed by a decrease.
source: Commonly, oligomycin results in a small increase in mitochondrial membrane potential, sometimes followed by a decrease (Kalbácová et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kalbácová et al., 2003 and Yang et al., 2021.

claim: Any quantitative effect of membrane potential on MTY fluorescence is negligible, unless the potential is completely lost, leading to dye leakage.
source: This implies that any quantitative effect of membrane potential on MTY fluorescence is negligible, unless the potential is completely lost, leading to dye leakage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and comparison with membrane potential studies.

claim: The excitation wavelength for gTEMP (360 nm) falls within the ultraviolet range, and the resulting cellular damage under continuous illumination for more than 60 min renders calibration unreliable.
source: The excitation wavelength for gTEMP (360 nm) falls within the ultraviolet range, and the resulting cellular damage under continuous illumination for more than 60 min renders calibration unreliable (Lu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2022.

claim: An alternative probe set, based on the recently developed B-gTEMP, should overcome the problem of UV damage in future studies.
source: An alternative probe set, based on the recently developed B-gTEMP (Lu et al., 2022), should overcome the problem in future studies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications, with citation to Lu et al., 2022.

claim: It was necessary to extrapolate the mito-gTEMP calibration curve beyond 42°C, assuming the linearity seen earlier for the isolated proteins.
source: One important caveat regarding the application of mito-gTEMP is that it was necessary to extrapolate the calibration curve beyond 42°C, assuming the linearity seen earlier for the isolated proteins (Nakano et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a methodological limitation, with citation to Nakano et al., 2017 for the linearity assumption.

claim: Above 42°C, in vivo calibration is not possible, due to the loss of cellular viability and integrity, accompanied by major changes in protein composition and distribution.
source: Above this temperature, in vivo calibration is not possible, due to the loss of cellular viability and integrity, accompanied by major changes in protein composition and distribution (Roti Roti, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Roti Roti, 2008 regarding cellular heat damage.

claim: The finding that mitochondrial temperature is of the order of 50°C or more and distinct from that of the rest of the cell has been challenged on both theoretical and experimental grounds.
source: The finding that mitochondrial temperature is of the order of 50°C or more and distinct from that of the rest of the cell has been challenged on both theoretical (Baffou et al., 2014) and experimental grounds (Moreno-Loshuertos et al., 2023).
evidence: This acknowledges challenges to the findings, with citations to Baffou et al., 2014 and Moreno-Loshuertos et al., 2023.

claim: Recent data indicate that the slow thermal diffusivity of mammalian cells is sufficient to account for the maintenance of intracellular temperature differences inferred under physiological conditions.
source: However, recent data indicate that the slow thermal diffusivity of mammalian cells (Lu et al., 2022) is sufficient to account for the maintenance of intracellular temperature differences inferred under physiological conditions and further documented here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2022.

claim: The maintenance of high mitochondrial temperature as a source of intracellular heat is supported by theoretical considerations.
source: Furthermore, the maintenance of high mitochondrial temperature as a source of intracellular heat is supported by theoretical considerations (Kang, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kang, 2018.

claim: The nucleus is 1–2°C warmer than the cytoplasm.
source: Some organelles or active regions manifest distinct temperature inhomogeneities: notably, the nucleus is 1–2°C warmer than the cytoplasm (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), the nucleolus even hotter (Piñol et al., 2020), and perinuclear mitochondria may be hotter than those at the cellular periphery (Savchuk et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Okabe et al., 2012 and Hayashi et al., 2015.

claim: The nucleolus is even hotter than the nucleus.
source: Some organelles or active regions manifest distinct temperature inhomogeneities: notably, the nucleus is 1–2°C warmer than the cytoplasm (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), the nucleolus even hotter (Piñol et al., 2020), and perinuclear mitochondria may be hotter than those at the cellular periphery (Savchuk et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piñol et al., 2020.

claim: Perinuclear mitochondria may be hotter than those at the cellular periphery.
source: Some organelles or active regions manifest distinct temperature inhomogeneities: notably, the nucleus is 1–2°C warmer than the cytoplasm (Okabe et al., 2012; Hayashi et al., 2015), the nucleolus even hotter (Piñol et al., 2020), and perinuclear mitochondria may be hotter than those at the cellular periphery (Savchuk et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Savchuk et al., 2019.

claim: Isolated OXPHOS complexes I and V are heat labile.
source: We previously reported (Chrétien et al., 2018) that isolated OXPHOS complexes I and V are heat labile, though OXPHOS complex II (cII), cIII, and cIV activities have temperature optima in the 50–55°C range when studied in intact mitochondrial membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chrétien et al., 2018.

claim: OXPHOS complex II (cII), cIII, and cIV activities have temperature optima in the 50–55°C range when studied in intact mitochondrial membranes.
source: We previously reported (Chrétien et al., 2018) that isolated OXPHOS complexes I and V are heat labile, though OXPHOS complex II (cII), cIII, and cIV activities have temperature optima in the 50–55°C range when studied in intact mitochondrial membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chrétien et al., 2018.

claim: The imposition of an external temperature of 43°C or above to cells or to isolated mitochondria damages respiratory function and disturbs OXPHOS complex and supercomplex organisation.
source: Others have recently reported that the imposition of an external temperature of 43°C or above to cells or to isolated mitochondria damages respiratory function and disturbs OXPHOS complex and supercomplex organisation (Moreno-Loshuertos et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moreno-Loshuertos et al., 2023.

claim: Externally applied heat delivered to mitochondria, which are already at elevated temperatures, may push them beyond their operational limit.
source: Thus, externally applied heat delivered to mitochondria, which our assays indicate are already at elevated temperatures, may push them beyond their operational limit, implying that mitochondrial heat production in vivo must be finely attuned to cellular needs, to avoid catastrophic overheating.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and cited literature on heat damage.

claim: Mitochondrial heat production in vivo must be finely attuned to cellular needs, to avoid catastrophic overheating.
source: Thus, externally applied heat delivered to mitochondria, which our assays indicate are already at elevated temperatures, may push them beyond their operational limit, implying that mitochondrial heat production in vivo must be finely attuned to cellular needs, to avoid catastrophic overheating.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings and considerations of heat damage.

claim: A recent meltome analysis of human proteins found that those constituting the respiratory chain complexes have median Tm values of around 60°C.
source: On the other hand, a recent meltome analysis of human proteins found that those constituting the respiratory chain complexes have median Tm values of around 60°C (Jarzab et al., 2020), consistent with our inference of high mitochondrial temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jarzab et al., 2020.

claim: Since rotenone and antimycin inhibition had the same mitochondrial temperature effect in iMEFs, both individually and in combination, electron flow entering the chain independently of cI in this cell background is negligible.
source: Since rotenone and antimycin inhibition had the same mitochondrial temperature effect in iMEFs, both individually and in combination, we infer that electron flow entering the chain independently of cI in this cell background is negligible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from iMEFs treated with different inhibitors.

claim: Around 20–30% of electron flow into cIII in U2OS cells must come from other ubiquinone-linked enzymes.
source: In contrast, antimycin produced a significantly greater mitochondrial temperature decrease in U2OS cells than did rotenone (Figure 2B), from which we conclude that around 20–30% of electron flow into cIII in this cell line must come from other ubiquinone-linked enzymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing rotenone and antimycin effects in U2OS cells, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In iMEFs and S2 cells, a measurable amount of electron flow to oxygen enters the OXPHOS system via cytochrome c independently of cIII, i.e., via the Mia40-Evr1/ALR protein import pathway.
source: In iMEFs (Figure 2C and D) and S2 cells (Figure 2E), though not in HEK293T or U2OS cells, KCN had a significantly greater mitochondrial temperature effect than antimycin, which implies that, in these cell lines, a measurable amount of electron flow to oxygen enters the OXPHOS system via cytochrome c independently of cIII, i.e., via the Mia40-Evr1/ALR protein import pathway, albeit that we were not able to verify this directly using the Evr1/ALR inhibitor MitoBloCK-6.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing KCN and antimycin effects, shown in Figure 2C, D, and E.

claim: cV itself must be able to generate some heat in the complete absence of cellular respiration, presumably by the hydrolysis of mitochondrially imported ATP.
source: In all cell lines that we were able to test, oligomycin produced a significantly greater mitochondrial temperature decrease than KCN (Figure 2A–D). Since KCN should block all respiratory proton pumping across the IMM, we infer that cV itself must be able to generate some heat in the complete absence of cellular respiration, presumably by the hydrolysis of mitochondrially imported ATP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing oligomycin and KCN effects, shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Residual thermogenesis from cV is inhibited by oligomycin and must involve cV in a reaction that is itself protonmotive.
source: Since this residual thermogenesis is inhibited by oligomycin, it must nevertheless involve cV, in a reaction that is itself protonmotive, and hence limited by the rate of dissipation of the IMM proton gradient by other processes, such as protein, metabolite, and ion transport.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of oligomycin effects.

claim: Rotenone inhibition of electron flow through cI initially produced the same temperature decrease in AOX-expressing iMEF mitochondria as in control iMEF mitochondria, which is consistent with the fact that AOX by-passes cIII+cIV but not cI.
source: Rotenone inhibition of electron flow through cI initially produced the same temperature decrease in AOX-expressing iMEF mitochondria as in control iMEF mitochondria (Figure 6A and B). This is consistent with the fact that AOX by-passes cIII+cIV but not cI (Dassa et al., 2009; McDonald and Gospodaryov, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B, and citations to Dassa et al., 2009 and McDonald and Gospodaryov, 2019.

claim: Electron flow through the inherently thermogenic AOX is expected substantially to replace the normal heating effect of electron flow through cIII+cIV.
source: In contrast, the mitochondrial temperature decrease produced by antimycin inhibition of cIII was substantially less than in control cells (Figure 6B). Electron flow through the inherently thermogenic AOX is expected substantially to replaces the normal heating effect of electron flow through cIII+cIV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and knowledge of AOX function.

claim: When cIII and cIV are able to function normally, electrons flowing through cI should not be diverted via AOX.
source: Note that, when cIII and cIV are able to function normally, electrons flowing through cI should not be diverted via AOX (Szibor et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szibor et al., 2020.

claim: The capacity of AOX to support electron flow from cI through to oxygen in iMEF cells remains below that of cIII+cIV.
source: Part of the explanation is that the capacity of AOX to support electron flow from cI through to oxygen in these cells remains below that of cIII+cIV, as inferred previously by respirometry (Giordano et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Giordano et al., 2019.

claim: The full engagement of AOX for cI-linked substrates requires the accumulation of ubiquinol, the reduced form of coenzyme Q.
source: Furthermore, the full engagement of AOX for cI-linked substrates (Szibor et al., 2020) requires the accumulation of ubiquinol, the reduced form of coenzyme Q.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szibor et al., 2020.

claim: The fact that the initial effect of KCN in AOX-expressing cells was greater than that caused by antimycin supports the idea that some of the electron flow through cIV in iMEFs is introduced via cytochrome c independently of cIII, for which AOX does not provide a by-pass.
source: The fact that the initial effect of KCN in AOX-expressing cells was greater than that caused by antimycin supports the idea that some of the electron flow through cIV in iMEFs is introduced via cytochrome c independently of cIII, for which AOX does not provide a by-pass.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing KCN and antimycin effects in AOX-expressing cells.

claim: The metabolic flexibility conferred by AOX may be important in maintaining mitochondrial temperature and organismal viability in the vast array of species that possess AOX but are subject to wide external temperature fluctuations.
source: Although AOX is not normally present in vertebrate cells, the metabolic flexibility that it confers may be important in maintaining mitochondrial temperature and organismal viability in the vast array of species that do possess AOX but are subject to wide external temperature fluctuations, namely bacteria, fungi, plants, eukaryotic protists, and many animals as well (McDonald and Gospodaryov, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings with AOX, with citation to McDonald and Gospodaryov, 2019 for the distribution of AOX.

claim: Rewarming in AOX-expressing cells should involve a remodelling of metabolism towards the oxidation of flavin-linked substrates that directly reduce ubiquinone.
source: Logically it should involve a remodelling of metabolism towards the oxidation of flavin-linked substrates that directly reduce ubiquinone.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the metabolic changes underlying the rewarming phenomenon.

claim: Rewarming in AOX-expressing cells does not involve the acquisition of additional capacity for AOX to receive electrons via cI.
source: Rewarming was evident in the case of cells in which cI was inhibited by rotenone (Figure 6A and C), indicting that it does not involve the acquisition of additional capacity for AOX to receive electrons via cI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation of rewarming in rotenone-treated AOX-expressing cells, shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: The efficient exchange of adenine nucleotides between mitochondria and the cytosol is not required for the maintenance of high mitochondrial temperature.
source: Thus, the efficient exchange of adenine nucleotides between mitochondria and the cytosol is not required for the maintenance of high mitochondrial temperature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations with BKA treatment.

claim: The usually minor contribution of intramitochondrial ATP turnover may be boosted sufficiently to drive mitochondrial heat production to near-normal levels after BKA treatment, possibly involving a contribution from cV-linked ATP hydrolysis.
source: Instead, the usually minor contribution of intramitochondrial ATP turnover may be boosted sufficiently to drive mitochondrial heat production to near-normal levels, possibly involving, once again, a contribution from cV-linked ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism of temperature maintenance after BKA treatment.

claim: Protein synthesis uses between 35% and 70% of the ATP produced in cells.
source: Protein synthesis uses between 35% and 70% of the ATP produced in cells (Stouthamer, 1973; Pontes et al., 2015; Siems et al., 1992; Rolfe and Brown, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stouthamer, 1973; Pontes et al., 2015; Siems et al., 1992; and Rolfe and Brown, 1997.

claim: Mitochondrial temperature maintenance in anisomycin-exposed iMEF cells is lower and less dependent on cI with time, yet remains fully dependent on cV.
source: Based on the inhibitor studies shown in Figure 7C and D, mitochondrial temperature maintenance in anisomycin-exposed iMEF cells is lower and less dependent on cI with time, yet remains fully dependent on cV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: As cellular ATP usage dwindles, cV may start to operate thermogenically as an ATPase.
source: This suggests that, as cellular ATP usage dwindles, cV may start to operate thermogenically as an ATPase, although this does not explain how the resulting proton gradient across the IMM is dissipated.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental observations with anisomycin treatment.

claim: A more complex mechanism, such as the futile creatine cycle recently documented in brown fat, may be involved in dissipating the proton gradient.
source: A more complex mechanism, such as the futile creatine cycle recently documented in brown fat (Rahbani et al., 2021), may need to be invoked.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion with citation to Rahbani et al., 2021.

claim: The adenine nucleotide carrier (ATP-Mg/Pi) may be involved in sustaining a futile cycle of intramitochondrial ATP hydrolysis, as well as possible reverse electron transport through cI.
source: The adenine nucleotide carrier (ATP-Mg/Pi), encoded by a small multigene family, which ensures the net delivery of adenine nucleotides to the mitochondrial matrix under specific physiological conditions (Fiermonte et al., 2004), may also be involved in sustaining a futile cycle of intramitochondrial ATP hydrolysis, as well as possible reverse electron transport through cI.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion with citation to Fiermonte et al., 2004.

claim: In anisomycin-exposed, AOX-expressing cells, where AOX itself provides an alternative mechanism of thermogenesis, cells remained more dependent on cI for the maintenance of high mitochondrial temperature over time.
source: In anisomycin-exposed, AOX-expressing cells, where AOX itself provides an alternative mechanism of thermogenesis, cells remained more dependent on cI for the maintenance of high mitochondrial temperature over time (Figure 7C), but less dependent on cV (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: A mitochondrial temperature in excess of 50°C places severe constraints on the mechanisms of intracellular heat conductance.
source: A mitochondrial temperature in excess of 50°C places severe constraints on the mechanisms of intracellular heat conductance.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration based on the experimental findings.

claim: Mitochondrial heat production must be responsive both to external heat stresses and to metabolic changes taking place within the cell, including those within the mitochondrion itself.
source: Here, we postulate that, at least in mammals, mitochondrial heat production sustains the cell broadly at around 37°C, but must be responsive both to external heat stresses and to metabolic changes taking place within the cell, including those within the mitochondrion itself.
evidence: This is a speculative postulate based on the experimental findings.

claim: The molecular and physical mechanisms that govern heat flow within and out of mitochondria must be both robust and flexible.
source: Thus, the molecular and physical mechanisms that govern heat flow within and out of mitochondria must be both robust and flexible.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings and theoretical considerations.

claim: The thermal conductivity of the mitochondrial membranes must be very small at the distances encountered in the cell between the hot and cold compartments.
source: As Fahimi and Matta, 2022, have pointed out, the thermal conductivity of the mitochondrial membranes must be very small at the distances encountered in the cell between the hot and cold compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fahimi and Matta, 2022.

claim: Fahimi and Matta offered a physical explanation for the mitochondrial paradox based on spikes in local temperature associated with proton passage from the IMS to the matrix.
source: Fahimi and Matta, 2022 termed this the mitochondrial paradox and offered a physical explanation based on spikes in local temperature associated with proton passage from the IMS to the matrix.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fahimi and Matta, 2022.

claim: Based on considerations of proton passage, Fahimi and Matta were able to predict a 7K difference across the mitochondrial membrane.
source: Based on these considerations they were able to predict a 7K difference across the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fahimi and Matta, 2022.

claim: The work of Fahimi and Matta is the only physically sound hypothesis yet proposed to account for the surprising temperature differences inferred experimentally.
source: To our knowledge, their work is the only physically sound hypothesis yet proposed, to account for the surprising temperature differences inferred experimentally, and whose validity has been widely debated (Lane, 2018; Baffou et al., 2014; Kiyonaka et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2015; Baffou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an evaluative statement with citations to the debate in the literature.

claim: The true efficiency of ATP synthase must be close to 90%, taking account of heat dissipation by informational transactions.
source: Matta and colleagues have also argued, based on thermodynamic principles (Matta and Massa, 2015), that the true efficiency of ATP synthase must be close to 90%, taking account of heat dissipation by informational transactions (Landauer's principle, Landauer, 1961) which is compensated by the inherent electrostatic potential of the enzyme (Vigneau et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matta and Massa, 2015; Landauer, 1961; and Vigneau et al., 2022.

claim: The additional temperature decrease produced by inhibiting ATP synthase in addition to inhibiting respiration is both small, but non-negligible, which may be partly explained by the high efficiency of ATP synthase.
source: This may partly explain why the additional temperature decrease produced by inhibiting ATP synthase in addition to inhibiting respiration is both small, but non-negligible.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the theoretical considerations to the experimental observations.

claim: The double membrane system of mitochondria may serve as an insulating layer enabling mitochondria to maintain a high internal temperature, whilst allowing the remainder of the cell to operate at a lower temperature.
source: Moreover, it suggests a novel role for the universal double membrane system of mitochondria, as an insulating layer enabling mitochondria to maintain a high internal temperature, whilst allowing the remainder of the cell to operate at a lower temperature.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings of high mitochondrial temperature.

claim: The ratio of mitochondrial volume to surface area may change in response to metabolic needs and physiological signals that regulate mitochondrial heat output.
source: If this is correct, a corollary is that the ratio of mitochondrial volume to surface area may change in response to metabolic needs and physiological signals that regulate mitochondrial heat output.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about mitochondrial dynamics based on the temperature findings.

claim: Mitochondria might be expected to fragment into smaller entities when heat output rises, so as to maintain internal mitochondrial temperature, and to fuse into filamentous structures when heat output is low.
source: Put more simply, mitochondria might be expected to fragment into smaller entities when heat output rises, so as to maintain internal mitochondrial temperature, and to fuse into filamentous structures when heat output is low.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the temperature findings and considerations of heat dissipation.

claim: Mitochondria may fragment if mitochondrial heat production is simply abolished and mitochondria need to absorb as much heat as possible from the rest of the cell, in order to maintain a minimal metabolism.
source: They may also fragment if mitochondrial heat production is simply abolished and mitochondria need to absorb as much heat as possible from the rest of the cell, in order to maintain a minimal metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Mitochondrial temperature homeostasis could be a determinant of the mitochondrial fusion/fission cycle.
source: The mitochondrial fusion/fission cycle has hitherto been associated primarily with mitochondrial quality control (Gottlieb et al., 2021), which is disturbed in patholological states and during aging (Seo et al., 2010). However, mitochondrial temperature homeostasis could also be a determinant.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion with citations to Gottlieb et al., 2021 and Seo et al., 2010.

claim: Inhibition of cV, but not of the other OXPHOS complexes, triggers mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: Accordingly, it has recently been reported that inhibition of cV, but not of the other OXPHOS complexes, triggers mitochondrial fragmentation (van der Stel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van der Stel et al., 2023.

claim: Treatment with rotenone or antimycin results in rapid depletion of intramitochondrial ATP.
source: Treatment with rotenone or antimycin were reported to result in rapid depletion of intramitochondrial ATP (van der Stel et al., 2023), consistent with our inference that these inhibitors allow some residual mitochondrial heat output driven by ATP hydrolysis, whilst oligomycin does not.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van der Stel et al., 2023.

claim: Using mito-gTEMP, treatment of cells with an uncoupler resulted in a mitochondrial temperature increase of ~6°C.
source: Using mito-gTEMP, it was previously shown that treatment of cells with an uncoupler, which is known to provoke mitochondrial fragmentation (Legros et al., 2002), also resulted in a mitochondrial temperature increase of ~6°C (see Figure 4 of Nakano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakano et al., 2017 and Legros et al., 2002.

claim: Using a different spectrophotometric method, the effect of a chemical uncoupler on mitochondrial temperature was estimated in the 4–5°C range.
source: Using a different spectrophotometric method, other authors estimated the effect of a chemical uncoupler in the 4–5°C range (Piñol et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piñol et al., 2020.

claim: U2OS was the cell line with the greatest inferred temperature difference between the two methods used to assess mitochondrial temperature, and also the one where this difference was the most variable experimentally.
source: Consistent with the idea that mitochondrial fusion is associated with low mitochondrial heat output, the cell line with the greatest inferred temperature difference between the two methods used in the present study to assess mitochondrial temperature, and also the one where this difference was the most variable experimentally, was U2OS (Figure 3E), a cell line in which mitochondria are mostly filamentous, e.g., see Westrate et al., 2014.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and citation to Westrate et al., 2014.

claim: In U2OS cells, mitochondria are mostly filamentous.
source: Consistent with the idea that mitochondrial fusion is associated with low mitochondrial heat output, the cell line with the greatest inferred temperature difference between the two methods used in the present study to assess mitochondrial temperature, and also the one where this difference was the most variable experimentally, was U2OS (Figure 3E), a cell line in which mitochondria are mostly filamentous, e.g., see Westrate et al., 2014.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Westrate et al., 2014.

claim: In iMEFs, mitochondria are highly fragmented under standard culture conditions.
source: In other cell lines, such as iMEFs, mitochondria are highly fragmented under standard culture conditions, e.g., see Abdullah et al., 2022.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Abdullah et al., 2022.

claim: Bright puncta observed in MTY-stained cells may correspond with nucleoids.
source: Staining of cells with MTY revealed bright puncta within mitochondria (Figure 4B), the nature of which is unknown. One possibility is that these may correspond with nucleoids.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the microscopy observations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae the orthologue of ALDH2 (Ald4) is a nucleoid protein.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae the orthologue of ALDH2 (Ald4) is a nucleoid protein (Kucej and Butow, 2007), but this has not been reported to be the case in mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kucej and Butow, 2007.

claim: The heat output of the OXPHOS system in bacteria should be similar to that of mitochondria.
source: Since the OXPHOS system is of bacterial origin, its heat output in bacteria should be similar to that of mitochondria, and we would expect that the thermal insulation provided in gram-negatives by the double membrane and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) cell wall, or by the thicker cell wall in gram-positives, should be at least as effective as that of the double membrane of mitochondria.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the evolutionary origin of mitochondria and the experimental findings.

claim: Intracellular temperature in bacteria is predicted to be some 15–20°C warmer than ambient temperature.
source: It will therefore be interesting to implement thermosensitive reporters such as gTEMP or B-gTEMP in bacteria, to assess intracellular temperature, which we would predict to be once again some 15–20°C warmer than ambient temperature.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the mitochondrial findings.

claim: A loss of mitochondrial heat generation activity, as in cases of mitochondrial disease, may compromise the maintenance of intracellular temperature or induce futile cycles of cytosolic ATP generation and usage that may have profound metabolic effects.
source: Similarly, considering that heat generation is an inescapable cellular function of metabolically active mitochondria, a loss of this activity, as in cases of mitochondrial disease, may compromise the maintenance of intracellular temperature or induce futile cycles of cytosolic ATP generation and usage that may have profound metabolic effects.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications for mitochondrial disease.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial heat generation could be a crucial aspect of mitochondrial pathology.
source: This could be a crucial aspect of mitochondrial pathology (Rango et al., 2014) and may also influence progression in other metabolic diseases, including cancer (El-Gammal et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion with citations to Rango et al., 2014 and El-Gammal et al., 2022.

claim: The maintenance of high mitochondrial temperature should be regarded as an important homeostatic process of the organelle, along with more traditionally considered parameters such as membrane potential, pH, ATP, metabolite levels, and ROS.
source: On the basis of our findings, we propose that the maintenance of high mitochondrial temperature should be regarded as an important homeostatic process of the organelle, along with more traditionally considered parameters such as membrane potential, pH, ATP, metabolite levels, and ROS.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings.
